slides.label: Exercises Become Diagnostics
slides.notes: Open by reframing the chapter. The source span is an exercise set, but this lecture treats the exercises as diagnostics for Act IV: transport, holonomy, curvature ledgers, geodesic deviation, tensor identity checks, and spacetime interpretation. Ask students to stop looking for isolated answers and instead ask what object is being tested, what measurement is being made, and what invariant should survive a change of representation.

slides.label: The Lab Grammar
slides.notes: Use the lab map to give students a stable method. Every problem family should move from an object to a visual model, then to a formula, and finally to a check. This prevents the common exercise-set failure mode where a formula is applied before the geometric object is clear. The instructor can ask the room to name the object before revealing each formula.

slides.label: Transport Is A Comparison Test
slides.notes: This slide makes parallel transport operational. A transported vector is not an arrow dragged across a drawing; it is a tangent vector compared by a connection along a path. The exercise diagnostic is to choose the curve, specify the comparison rule, and predict what should happen under rerouting, shrinking a loop, or changing coordinates.

slides.label: Holonomy Turns Loops Into Curvature
slides.notes: Move from along-path comparison to loop comparison. Holonomy asks whether a vector returns to its starting tangent plane with the same direction after being transported around a closed curve. For a tiny loop the returned angle divided by enclosed area estimates curvature, so the problem becomes a meter rather than a symbolic ritual.

slides.label: Boundary Curvature Has To Be Accounted For
slides.notes: Use the sphere-cone artifact as a warning that curvature accounting has several entries. An angle excess or defect is not only an interior curvature story; boundary geodesic curvature and corner turns may also contribute. Good solutions state which entries are present, which vanish, and which sign convention is being used.

slides.label: Gauss-Bonnet Is A Ledger
slides.notes: The local Gauss-Bonnet calculator makes the bookkeeping global. The topology number on the right side is fixed, while the curvature integral, boundary turning, and corner terms can trade value under deformation. Exercises in this family are best read as conservation laws: find the missing entry and verify the total against Euler characteristic.

slides.label: Geodesic Deviation Reads Curvature Dynamically
slides.notes: Connect Act IV transport to neighboring geodesics. A Jacobi field is a moving separation vector along a base geodesic, and the curvature tensor supplies the relative acceleration term. The diagnostic question is whether nearby geodesics coast, focus, or spread. Students should predict the qualitative behavior before manipulating the tensor formula.

slides.label: Tensor Identities Are Regression Tests
slides.notes: Treat the Riemann and Bianchi identities as consistency tests rather than decoration. The tensor has symmetries because it records a geometric failure of comparisons to commute, not because an array happens to have repeated entries. The heatmap stands in for a symbolic regression check: if a computed tensor violates these identities, the connection or index convention is suspect.

slides.label: Spacetime Uses The Same Diagnostic Habit
slides.notes: The relativity exercises extend the same Act IV grammar into spacetime. Free-fall worldlines are geodesics, tidal acceleration is geodesic deviation, and the Einstein tensor packages curvature into a divergence-free source ledger. The goal is not to solve field equations on a slide, but to recognize the same object-measurement-invariant habit in Lorentzian geometry.

slides.label: The Act IV Exercise Playbook
slides.notes: Close by turning the whole chapter into a reusable playbook. For any exercise, students should write four columns: object, measurement, invariant, and pitfall. Transport checks compare tangent vectors, holonomy checks returned angles, Gauss-Bonnet checks curvature budgets, Jacobi checks relative acceleration, tensor checks identities, and spacetime checks conservation and tidal interpretation.
